from  within  to  without  the  horopter  circle, 
and  reversely,  by  altering  the  relative  bright 
ness  of  its  nasal  and  temporal  half-images. 
From  all  this  it  follows  (and  most  conclu- 


sively  from  the  last  consideration)  that  differ 
ences  in  retinal  images  are  sufficient  of  them 


selves  to  mediate  the  perception  of  solidity 
(AVundt,  Physiol.  Psi/chol.,  4th  ed.,  ii.  227). 

There  are  other  methods  by  which  pictures 
in  two  dimensions  can  be  represented  to  the 
eye  in  relief,  (i)  If  a  right-hand  view  in  red 
is  superimposed  in  the  printing  upon  a  left- 
hand  view  in  blue,  and  if  the  eyes  are  fur 
nished  with  spectacles  consisting  of  blue  glass 
for  the  right  eye  and  red  glass  for  the  left 
eye,  two  black  images  are  produced  which 
are  suitable  for  binocular  fusion  into  a  single 
three-dimensional  impression  (method  in 
vented  by  L.  D.  du  Hauron  of  Algiers  ;  mate 
rials  and  slides  sold  by  the  Comptoir  Suisse 
de  Photographic,  Geneva,  and  by  Williams, 
Brown,  &  Earle,  Philadelphia).  (2)  Polar- 
i/.ed  light  also  furnishes  a  method  of  giving 
different  appropriate  images  to  the  two  eyes, 
and,  like  the  last-mentioned,  it  is  adapted  to 
representation  in  the  lecture  room.  By  means 
of  a  double  lantern,  two  pictures  are  thrown 
together  upon  a  screen  by  two  beams  of  white 
light  polari/ed  in  planes  at  right  angles  to 


each  other,  and  each  person  in  the  audience 
is  furnished  with  eye-glasses  consisting  of  a 
pair  of  analysers.  (This  apparatus  was  in 
vented  by,  and  may  lie  obtained  from,  John 
Anderton,  of  Birmingham,  England.)  (O.L.F.) 
The  reflecting  stereoscope  was  invented  by 
Wheatstone  (described  1833  a"d  ^S^);  the 
current  form  of  the  refracting  stereoscope 
(also  first  described  by  Wheatstone)  is  due  to 
Brewster  (1843).

Sterility  [Lat.  sterilis,  barren] :  Gler. 
Unfruchtbarkeit ;  Fr.  sterilite ;  Ital.  steiilita, 
infeconditck.  The  condition  of  not  producing 
young  ;  infertility. 

In  botany,  male  flowers  (having  stamens 
only)  are  termed  sterile.  In  female  animals 
sterility  may  be  due  to  inability  to  produce  ova, 
or  in  the  higher  forms  to  inability  to  sustain 
the  ova  until  birth,  or  to  some  obstruction  to 
the  actual  impregnation  of  the  ova.  (c.s.M.) 
The  principal  biological  question  in  con 
nection  with  sterility  is  that  of  the  mutual 
infertility  of  species  with  one  another.  Dar 
win  supposed  this  sterility  of  species  inter  se 
to  be  a  result  of  divergent  evolution  produced 
by  other  causes ;  Romanes  reverses  the  case, 
and  in  his  hypothesis  of  PHYSIOLOGICAL 
SELECTION  (q.  v.)  makes  variations  towards
